newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Holbrooke's pickings in Belgrade slim - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke's pickings in Belgrade slim - analysts.

text.p: U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke has gained little from his visit to Belgrade, apart from a promise indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic would finally disappear from Bosnian politics, analysts said on Sunday.

Momcilo Krajisnik, the hardline Serb member of the Bosnian presidency, had "offered a unilateral undertaking" to fulfil a July 1996 agreement which the former Bosnian Serb leader Karadzic had "shredded", Holbrooke said.
Holbrooke, the architect of the 1995 Dayton peace accord which ended the wars in Bosnia and Croatia, on Saturday gave Serb leaders a period of grace to remove Karadzic in order to avoid bloodshed.
Analysts and diplomats said this would shore up Krajisnik's position as the leading hardline figure battling pro-Dayton Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic.
It also cemented Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic's position as the pivotal political powerbroker in the region.
"It ended up with Serbs vs Yanks, 2-0," one western diplomat said.
Holbrooke admitted the United States would not be satisfied until Karadzic was brought to justice before the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

Sources close to the negotiations said Washington had accepted the deal in order to avoid the bloodshed many fear would result if NATO-led troops in Bosnia moved to arrest Karadzic, who is guarded by hundreds of men.

"We are still offering an easy way out. If the Bosnian Serbs do not accept it then we will use other effective means," a source close to the talks in Belgrade said, noting that NATO commander General Wesley Clark had been asked to join the talks with Krajisnik by telephone.
Under a deal Holbrooke brokered last year with Milosevic and Krajisnik, Karadzic stepped down as Bosnian Serb president and was supposed to stay out of politics.
But he has violated the deal and still rules with an iron fist the Serb-controlled half of Bosnia, persistently circumventing the Dayton peace accords and undermining Plavsic.

Holbrooke travelled to Banja Luka, Plavsic's headquarters, to show his support for the woman who has publicly accused Karadzic of violating the Dayton accords to continue looting Bosnian Serb territory with impunity.
Krajisnik, the most powerful man in the Bosnian Serb republic after Karadzic, was not known for keeping his promises during the 3-1/2 year Bosnian war, the diplomat noted.

"Holbrooke has made a serious mistake by allowing Krajisnik to make the promise. It gives him greater maneouvering space and shores up his position as a man in charge of implementing the Dayton peace accords," Brana Milosevic, a senior Belgrade political analyst told Reuters.

"On the other hand, Milosevic has deftly appointed his man to do the job and saved his position as the regional power broker (who is) never directly responsible for whatever happens on the ground," he said.
Sources close to the negotiations said Holbrooke and Milosevic spent about 90 minutes alone on Friday.
"It is too early to tell whether...Holbrooke delivered a final warning to Milosevic -- We are coming to get Karadzic. But for sure Milosevic would have fought to avoid that," the diplomat said.
"Whatever was said, it sent Krajisnik scampering to Belgrade the next day."
The NATO-led peace force in Bosnia has recently changed tactics and actively sought out war criminals who avoided extradition to The Hague.
Troops of the Stabilisation Force (SFOR) captured one and shot dead another in Prijedor last month.
SFOR commander U.S. General Eric Shinseki has said the force would also take action against unauthorised special police units, such as the ones guarding Karadzic.

"It appears that Karadzic's time is running out. The maneouvre with Krajisnik does spare Americans from inflicting or sustaining injuries, but leaves both Milosevic and Krajisnik in strong positions," the diplomat said.
